title: Precision, Recall & F1
hook: On rare events, a model can be 99% accurate and still useless. Precision and recall reveal what accuracy hides.
key_points: Accuracy misleads on imbalanced data — always predicting the majority class can look great.
Precision: of the items you flagged positive, how many really were?
Recall: of all the real positives out there, how many did you catch?
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, rewarding a balance of both.
content_html: When the classes you're predicting are lopsided — say, rare diseases or fraud — plain accuracy can be high while the model misses everything that matters. Precision and recall split the question apart: precision asks how trustworthy your positive predictions are, recall asks how many of the true positives you found. F1 combines them into one number.
extra_html:
How it works

Precision is true positives divided by everything you predicted positive, so it punishes false alarms. Recall is true positives divided by all actual positives, so it punishes misses. The two trade off: cast a wide net and recall rises while precision falls, and vice versa. F1, the harmonic mean of the two, stays low unless both are reasonably high, which is why it's a popular single-number summary.

Why it matters

Choosing the right metric is choosing what kind of mistake you can live with. A cancer screen wants high recall even at the cost of false alarms; a spam filter may favor precision so it doesn't trash real mail. Reporting accuracy alone on imbalanced data is one of the easiest ways to be misled.
